title: Dear Wendy
full_review:
If you own a gun, it's bound to end badly, yessiree. That, in a nutshell, would seem to be the message of Danish filmmaker Thomas Vinterberg's second English-language feature.

The offbeat, sometimes compelling, but ultimately puzzling "Dear Wendy" (Wellspring) is set in an unspecified American mining town, where young Dick (Jamie Bell) is hoping he won't have to follow his father as a miner. Thanks to the intervention of his strong-willed nanny, Clarabelle (Novella Nelson), he doesn't.

When his father dies, Dick settles into a solitary existence, until one day he's visited by his friend, Stevie (Mark Webber), another loner who instills in Dick a love of guns' history and craftsmanship.

Dick had, years ago, bought what he thought was a fake gun from local toy shop sales gal Susan (Alison Pill), but now Stevie informs Dick that the revolver is real and explains its historical background. Dick christens the gun "Wendy" and speaks to it lovingly as if it were human.

Dick and Stevie eventually gather all the outcast teenagers -- Susan from the toy store, the legless Huey (Chris Owen), Huey's young brother, Freddie (Michael Angarano), the school punching bag -- for a secret society of gun aficionados who dress in period garb and hold meetings in an abandoned mine where they re-enact ancient rituals, practice shooting with their antique guns, and call themselves "Dandies."

All of them are steadfastly "pacifist" by nature, and they have absolutely no desire to use the weapons for violent means.

One day, Krugsby (Bill Pullman), the local sheriff, tells Dick he is to be the unofficial probation officer to Clarabelle's nephew, Sebastian (Danso Gordon), a youth who's run afoul of the law. Dick takes on this charge reluctantly, and before long he brings Sebastian into the Dandies.

Sebastian thinks they're all crazy but he goes along with it, and in fact shows such prowess with a gun that he makes Dick jealous.

Sebastian reveals that his aunt is now a recluse, going out only one day a year to visit her cousin across the square, but this year she's too afraid to do even that. Dick decides the group will form a protective cordon for his old nanny and bring her to her cousin safely.

Let's just say things don't work out as planned.

Vinterberg skillfully shows how these lonely teenagers become enamored of guns and, though never intending to use them for violent means, are swept up in the weapons' mystique and power. It's a highly intriguing premise, with parallels on a global scale, but the picture falls far short of gripping.

The measured pacing is often downright slow, and the deliberately artificial setup is off-putting. (The town square almost seems like a stage set, and the film was actually shot in Denmark and Germany.)

The English Bell is outstanding (speaking with yet another flawless American accent as he did in "The Chumscrubber") and it's partly his hypnotic narration -- a letter to the anthropomorphized "Wendy" -- that makes the unpleasant yarn as palatable as it is, while the others are fine, too.

The theme is one of anti-guns and anti-violence, and though it's reasonably clear what Vinterberg (and scriptwriter Lars Von Trier) are trying to say, the film's inevitable bloodbath ending is unsatisfying, even if, realistically, it's the only way the plot could go.

This "Wendy" is definitely not for the "Peter Pan" crowd.

The film contains profanity and rough language, violence and bloodshed. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
